{"id": "11:54/q24", "question": "Should recitation pause at the end of this verse despite the continuing syntax?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:54/q24/p1", "position": "Yes; verse endings merit a pause even where grammar continues into the next verse.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites 11:55 and 40:71–73 as syntactically continuous across boundaries. He says fawāṣil contribute to inimitability and eloquence, and pausing lets their patterned sounds work on listeners; missing such endings spoils poetic rhyme or sajʿ, and explaining meaning belongs to a lecturer rather than overriding a reciter's craft. Some authorities, transmitted via al-Itqan from Abu Amr, call pausing at verse ends Sunnah; al-Bayhaqi's Shuʿab al-Iman prefers it even across connected syntax; Umm Salama's report in Abu Dawud describes the Prophet pausing verse by verse."}]}

{"id": "11:55/q03", "question": "Whom does Hūd challenge to plot?", "turns_on": "Whether the idols share the direct grammatical address or are brought into a challenge directed to their worshippers.", "positions": [{"id": "11:55/q03/p1", "position": "His people together with their gods or idols, and all who stand with them.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Wahidi, Baghawi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Jawzi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Ibn Kathir, Alusi, Elmalili, Tabatabai, and Study Quran include people and idols. {"id": "11:55/q04", "question": "What action does Hūd tell them to take against him?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:55/q04/p1", "position": "They should unite in a hostile plot and attempt whatever harm, even killing, they can.", "reasons": "Wahidi Basit mentions hostility, anger, or striking him; Baydawi mentions trying to kill him. {"id": "11:55/q05", "question": "What does the command to plot imply about their power to harm Hūd?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative asserts that harm is impossible or only that Hūd does not fear possible harm; Tabatabai tests this by the following declaration of reliance on God.", "positions": [{"id": "11:55/q05/p1", "position": "It is a taunting, impossible challenge exposing their inability.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls the imperative permission used as a taunt, comparing 77:39 and refuting 11:54. Tabatabai calls both imperatives deliberately impossible; the gods cannot harm or avenge themselves, and even the strong people cannot kill or punish him. Alusi reasons that powerful people's inability makes the idols' inability still clearer; Nasafi rejects the claim that idols made Hūd mad."}, {"id": "11:55/q05/p2", "position": "Hūd declares his fearlessness even supposing they can harm him.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reports this possible reading, comparing the magicians' words to Pharaoh in 20:72, but says Hūd's subsequent reliance on God rules it out."}]}

{"id": "11:55/q13", "question": "Why is the full first-person yā used here in comparison with Aʿrāf?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:55/q13/p1", "position": "The longer form suits Hūd's longer, more intense confrontation and repeated first-person yā.", "reasons": "Samarrai contrasts this open challenge with the less confrontational setting in Aʿrāf 7:194–195, observes a longer exchange here and repeated first-person yā in 11:54–57 versus one instance at 7:196, and says full yā generally accompanies detailed contexts while kasra replacing it accompanies concise expression, apart from verse endings and vocatives. {"id": "11:84/q11", "question": "What wrongdoing does the prohibition on measure and balance describe?", "turns_on": "Notes distinguish giving customers less from manipulating measuring instruments, and some include taking excess.", "positions": [{"id": "11:84/q11/p1", "position": "They gave less than people's due in measure or weight.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī describes deprivation of due shares.
